blog_summary: Adrian Colyer reviews a 2016 paper demonstrating the Hierarchical Temporal Memory (HTM) neural network model's capabilities in continuous online sequence learning. The paper highlights HTM's strengths in handling real-time streaming data, including its ability to learn in a single pass without buffering, make higher-order predictions across multiple time steps, handle multiple simultaneous predictions, and exhibit robustness to sensor noise and fault tolerance. Notably, HTM achieves comparable accuracy to state-of-the-art algorithms like LSTMs without requiring task-specific hyperparameter tuning. The blog post emphasizes HTM's unique properties, such as sparse distributed representations (SDRs) and local learning rules, which contribute to its performance and adaptability. The paper also explores HTM's application to predicting New York City taxi passenger demand, further validating its practical utility.
paper_title: Continuous online sequence learning with an unsupervised neural network model
paper_abstract: The ability to recognize and predict temporal sequences of sensory inputs is vital for survival in natural environments. Based on many known properties of cortical neurons, hierarchical temporal memory (HTM) sequence memory is recently proposed as a theoretical framework for sequence learning in the cortex. In this paper, we analyze properties of HTM sequence memory and apply it to sequence learning and prediction problems with streaming data. We show the model is able to continuously learn a large number of variable-order temporal sequences using an unsupervised Hebbian-like learning rule. The sparse temporal codes formed by the model can robustly handle branching temporal sequences by maintaining multiple predictions until there is sufficient disambiguating evidence. We compare the HTM sequence memory with other sequence learning algorithms, including statistical methods: autoregressive integrated moving average (ARIMA), feedforward neural networks: online sequential extreme learning machine (ELM), and recurrent neural networks: long short-term memory (LSTM) and echo-state networks (ESN), on sequence prediction problems with both artificial and real-world data. The HTM model achieves comparable accuracy to other state-of-the-art algorithms. The model also exhibits properties that are critical for sequence learning, including continuous online learning, the ability to handle multiple predictions and branching sequences with high order statistics, robustness to sensor noise and fault tolerance, and good performance without task-specific hyperparameters tuning. Therefore the HTM sequence memory not only advances our understanding of how the brain may solve the sequence learning problem, but is also applicable to a wide range of real-world problems such as discrete and continuous sequence prediction, anomaly detection, and sequence classification.
